COMPTROLLER’S DECISION

This decision is considered final on January 29, 2024 unless a motion for rehearing is timely filed; this date of finality is calculated based on the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).[1] The failure to timely file a motion for rehearing may result in adverse legal consequences.

Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Kathy Pickup of the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) issued a Proposal for Decision (PFD) that includes Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law. SOAH served the PFD on each party and each party was given an opportunity to file exceptions and replies with SOAH in accordance with SOAH’s rules of procedure. The ALJ recommended that the Comptroller adopt the PFD as written.

After review and consideration, IT IS ORDERED that the PFD is adopted as written.

The results from this Decision are Attachments A. The ALJ’s recommendation letter is Attachment B. The PFD as written is Attachment C. Attachments A, B, and C are incorporated by reference.

Attachments A reflects a liability.[2]

The total sum of the tax, penalty, and interest is due and payable 20 days after a comptroller’s decision becomes final.[3] If such sum is not timely paid, an additional penalty of 10 percent of the taxes due will accrue.

TEXAS COMPTROLLER OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS

Proposal for Decision

The Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) audited ************** (Petitioner) for compliance with mixed beverage tax laws and sales tax laws and made three assessments: one for mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT), one for mixed beverage sales tax (MBST), and one for sales and use tax. Each assessment included tax, 10% late penalty, and accrued interest. The MBST and MBGRT assessments also included a 50% fraud penalty. Petitioner requested redetermination for each hearing. Petitioner raised no specific contentions in relation to the sales and use tax assessment but disagreed with the audit methodology and contended general audit error for the MBST and MBGRT assessments. In this Proposal for Decision (PFD), the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) finds that the assessments, including the 50% fraud penalties, should be upheld.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on June 15, 2023, issued Notices of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. On June 16, 2023, ALJ Kathy Pickup issued an order setting the written submission hearing and combining the cases for purposes of issuing a single PFD. Petitioner subsequently filed an agreed motion to convert to an in-person hearing, which was granted. Janice Cahalane represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by its managing member, **************. The hearing convened on November 29, 2023. The record closed on December 1, 2023, after the parties filed the evidence that was admitted at the hearing.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction in this proceeding. Therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE

Petitioner submitted sales reports and complimentary drink reports for January 1, 2019, through March 15, 2022.

Staff presented the testimony of the auditor, INDIVIDUAL and submitted the following exhibits for each hearing:

1. Hearing Request Receipt Letters;

2. Texas Notifications of Audit Results;

3. Penalty and Interest Waiver Worksheets;

4. Audit Package (MBGRT);

5. Audit Documentation Report / Audit Plan (MBGRT);

6. Audit Package (MBST);

7. Audit Documentation Report / Audit Plan (MBST);

8. Audit Package (Sales and Use Tax);

9. Audit Documentation Report / Audit Plan (Sales and Use Tax);

10. Audit Referral Report for Additional Penalty (Mixed Beverage Taxes);

11. Posts from Petitioner’s Facebook Page;

12. Posts from Petitioner’s Facebook Page for Periods from November 2020 to September 2021; and

13. Vendor-Reported Purchase Data Summay for the Tax Period.

The parties’ exhibits were admitted without objection.

B. AGREED ADJUSTMENTS

Staff did not agree to amend any of the assessments.

C. MATERIAL FACTS

During the period at issue, Petitioner held a mixed beverage permit and a sales and use tax permit, and operated a sports bar, COMPANY, in CITY, Texas. The bar also sold food items.

In August 2021, Staff initiated a MBGRT, MBST, and sales tax audit of Petitioner for the period January 1, 2018, through September 30, 2021. At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit. Petitioner did not provide any records.

A depletion analysis was performed based on the average serving size for distilled spirits and beer and vendor-reported purchases. The auditor conducted a pour test on August 26, 2021. During the pour observation, the auditor tested five drinks, which resulted in an average pour of 1.41 ounces for distilled spirits and 14.88 ounces for beer.[4] Using the serving sizes and Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits and beer available for sale during the audit period. Due to the lack of documentation provided by Petitioner, the auditor used prices obtained from the pour test observation to determine the average selling price, then multiplied those prices by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer. Petitioner did not provide the auditor with documentation of complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, theft, breakage, or other potential allowances.

The differences between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for each beverage category. The auditor applied the respective underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from sales of distilled spirits and beer for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. The applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due.

On March 14, 2022, Staff issued Texas Notifications of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing liabilities for MBGRT and MBST. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for sales and use tax. All assessments included tax, a 10% penalty, and accrued interest. The MBGRT and MBST assessments also included a 50% additional penalty. The overall error rate in reporting tax was 65.41% for MBST and 64.66% for MBGRT. Petitioner had 37 late returns during the audit period for MBGRT and 36 late returns for MBST.

Petitioner requested redetermination, disagreeing with the audit methodology used and contending general audit error for the MBST and MBGRT assessments. Petitioner did not provide any records and did not raise any specific contentions in relation to the sales and use tax assessment. Staff contends no adjustments are warranted and referred the matters to SOAH.

D. ALJ’S ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. “Taxable items” include tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010. The law requires retailers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

In addition to the sales tax due on taxable items, a 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001. In addition, an 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

As a mixed beverage permit holder, Petitioner was required to maintain records that reflected the purchases, sales, and gross receipts from the sale or service of alcoholic beverages. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(j)‑(m), .1002(c)(4). In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the gross receipts tax and sales tax liability based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. Id. §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. Id. Thus, mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See id.; Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017). The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011). Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation.[5] Mixed beverage audits performed in accordance with proper auditing practices and procedures, based upon the best information available, are presumed to be correct. Comptroller’s Decision No. 41,997 (2004).

Petitioner states it did not report sales from April 2020 to September 2021 because it was closed due to the pandemic. However, Staff provided evidence of Petitioner’s Facebook posts for periods from November 2020 to September 2021 (Staff’s Exhibit No. 12) with a summary of Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchase data for that period (Staff’s Exhibit No. 13) reflecting that it was open for business along. In addition, the pour test that was conducted during this time.

The assessments at issue were based upon Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages and a pour test conducted at the bar. The ALJ finds that Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that the audit was based on the best information available. Therefore, Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to demonstrate that the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e). Petitioner submitted very limited evidence for the joined hearing and, therefore, the ALJ finds Petitioner failed to establish error in the audit. The sales and use tax, MBST, and MBGRT assessments should be upheld in their entirety.

Texas Tax Code § 111.061(b) authorizes a 50% penalty when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. Id. § 1.26(b)(1). Clear and convincing evidence is evidence demonstrating that the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

The Comptroller has repeatedly held that gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, sufficiently indicates intent to evade the tax and warrants the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015). The Tax Code defines gross error to mean that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b). The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019). Negligence, whether slight or great, is not the equivalent of fraud with intent to evade tax. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 45,514 (2006), 42,244 (2003), 38,886 (2002), 37,555 (1999), 35,527 (1997), 33,554 (1995); see also Webb v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 394 F.2d 366 (5th Cir. 1968).

In this case, Petitioner’s overall error rates for MBGRT and MBST are both in excess of 64%, and Petitioner did not provide a plausible explanation for the gross underreporting. Therefore, Staff’s evidence is sufficient to support the application of the 50% penalty for the MBGRT and MBST assessments.

In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011). The same principle applies to a limited liability company. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 112,305, 112,307, and 112,308 (2016). The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a). To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. Id. § 3.15(b). The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. Id. § 3.15(c).

************** is the managing member of Petitioner and prepared and filed the MBGRT and MBST returns at issue. There is no evidence that the fraudulent tax returns were due to an independent course of conduct taken by either ************** or any of Petitioner’s employees that did not further any purpose of Petitioner, and Petitioner has not produced any evidence to demonstrate that the acts or omissions of its officers, managers, and employees should not be imputed to Petitioner. The 50% penalty should be upheld for the MBGRT and MBST assessments.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. During the period at issue, ************** (Petitioner) held a mixed beverage permit and a sales and use tax permit, and operated a bar as COMPANY, in CITY, Texas.

2. ************** is the managing member of Petitioner and prepared and filed the mixed beverage sales tax (MBST) and mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT) returns for Petitioner.

3. In August 2021, the Tax Division (Staff) or the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) initiated an MBGRT, MBST, and sales and use tax audit of Petitioner for the period January 1, 2018, through September 30, 2021.

4. At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit.

5. The auditor conducted the audit by performing a depletion analysis based on the average serving size for distilled spirits and beer, (calculated through a pour test performed at the bar) and vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverage inventory.

6. Petitioner did not provide any records in response to the auditor’s request but subsequently provided sales reports and complimentary drinks reports for January 1, 2019, through March 15, 2022.

7. The auditor conducted a pour test on August 26, 2021. During the pour observation, the auditor tested five drinks, which resulted in an average pour of 1.41 ounces for distilled spirits and 14.88 ounces for beer. Wine sales were deemed immaterial.

8. Using the serving sizes and Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits and beer available for sale during the audit period.

9. The auditor used prices obtained from the pour test observation to determine the average selling price (ASP) and multiplied the ASP by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer.

10. Petitioner did not provide documentation showing complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, theft, breakage, or other potential allowances.

11. The differences between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for each beverage category.

12. The auditor applied the respective underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from sales of distilled spirits and beer for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. The applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due.

13. On March 14, 2022, Staff issued Texas Notifications of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing liabilities for MBGRT and MBST. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for sales and use tax. All assessments included tax, a 10% penalty, and accrued interest. The MBGRT and MBST assessments also included a 50% additional penalty.

14. The overall error rate in reporting tax was 65.41% for MBST and 64.66% for MBGRT.

15. Petitioner had 37 late returns during the audit period for MBGRT and 36 late returns for MBST.

16. Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessments.

17. Petitioner did not provide any records and did not raise any specific contentions in relation to the sales and use tax assessment.

18. Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

19. On June 15, 2023, Staff issued Notices of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. The notices contained a statement of the nature of the hearings; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearings were to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaints or petitions filed with the state agency.

20. On June 16, 2023, the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) issued an order which combined the cases for purposes of issuing a single Proposal for Decision.

21. Petitioner subsequently filed an agreed motion to convert to an in-person hearing, which was granted.

22. The hearing convened on November 29, 2023.

23. The contested case record closed on December1, 2023, after the parties filed the evidence that was admitted at the hearing.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over these matters. Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to these hearings, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearings. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. “Taxable items” include tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010. The law requires retailers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

5. A 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001.

6. An 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

7. A mixed beverage permittee is a person, agent, or the officer, director, manager, or managing general partner of an entity that is the holder of a mixed beverage permit, a mixed beverage late hours permit, a mixed beverage permit holding a food and beverage certificate, a daily temporary mixed beverage permit, a private club registration permit, a private club exemption certificate permit, a private club late hours permit, a daily temporary private club permit, a private club registration permit holding a food and beverage certificate, a caterer’s permit, or a rectifier’s and distiller’s permit issued by the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Commission. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001(a)(8).

8. As a mixed beverage permittee, Petitioner was required to maintain records that reflected the purchases, sales, and gross receipts from the sale or service of alcoholic beverages. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(j)‑(m), .1002(c)(4).

9. In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the MBGRT and MBST liability based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

10. The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

11. Mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 115,139 and 115,140 (2019); Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017).

12. The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011).

13. Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation. See Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017) at 24.

14. Mixed beverage audits performed in accordance with proper auditing practices and procedures, based upon the best information available, are presumed to be correct. See Comptroller’s Decision No. 41,997 (2004).

15. Staff established, prima facie, that the assessments were based on the best information available.

16. Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to substantiate claims the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e).

17. Petitioner failed to establish error in the assessments.

18. A 50% penalty is authorized when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Tex. Tax Code § 111.061(b).

19. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(b)(1).

20. Clear and convincing evidence demonstrates the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

21. Gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, is sufficiently indicative of intent to evade the tax to warrant the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015).

22. Gross error means that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b).

23. The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019).

24. Petitioner did not provide a plausible explanation for the gross underreporting of MBGRT and MBST.

25. Staff’s evidence is sufficient to demonstrate, clearly and convincingly, that the 50% penalty applied to the MBGRT and MBST assessments is authorized by statute.

26. In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011).

27. The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a).

28. To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(b).

29. The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(c).

30. Petitioner did not produce evidence to demonstrate that the acts or omissions of its officers, managers, and employees should not be imputed to Petitioner.

31. The 50% penalty should be upheld for the MBGRT and MBST assessments.

SIGNED December 4, 2023.

KATHY PICKUP

PRESDING ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE
